newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Impact of Dutch bank reserves data not yet clear.
newsitem.headline: Impact of Dutch bank reserves data not yet clear.

text.p: The decision by Dutch banks to unveil their hidden reserves has sparked a debate among analysts on whether it will boost profits.

Analysts are divided on whether ABN AMRO and ING Groep will cut their total risk provisioning once they have revealed the size of the reserves, which is expected to show they have over-provided for bad loans in the past.
While some brokers expect total profits and earnings per share (EPS) to be higher as a result of lower future provisions, others see growth in EPS or in total profits.
Banking is the only sector in the Netherlands allowed to create hidden reserves and provisions but, ahead of changes to EU guidelines, Dutch banks have decided to reveal them.
The provision for general risks (VAR) will be announced by ABN AMRO on February 27 and by ING on April 3 with their respective 1996 annual results.
Some brokers last year calculated the effects of the new accounting move but stockbroker ABN AMRO Hoare Govett, a unit of ABN AMRO, revived the issue with a report earlier this month.
"It's old news but it does stimulate the (share) price," said Daan Worm of ING Barings.
In the report, ABN AMRO Hoare Govett analysts Margot van der Velden and Bryan Crossley said total risk provisioning would fall as from 1997, leading to higher earnings and dividends.
They estimated this would add 5-8 percent to ING's 1997 EPS and dividends per share above their current estimates of 4.65 and 2.00 cents respectively.
"The unveiling of the bank's hidden reserves should create significant upside potential for share prices in the sector," they said in the report.
Analysts estimate ABN AMRO's VAR at 4-5 billion guilders with ING's reserves put at 3.5-4.4 billion.
"I think there'll be a positive effect. I don't think they will keep provisions at the same levels," Jean-Paul van Bavel of Van Lanschot Bankiers said.

He said this meant EPS growth in 1997 would be eight percent for ABN AMRO, compared with three percent without the accounting changes, while for ING growth would be 7-8 percent, versus five percent under the old system.
"You are also seeing autonomous growth," he added.
ING Barings' Woorm said the hidden reserves grew during the 1980s as provisions for possible loan losses exceeded actual losses.
"You can't escape the fact that risk provisioning has been used to smooth the cyclical development of profits," he said.
He estimated ABN AMRO's 1997 EPS at 10.30 cents, 8-10 percent higher than if the changes had not occurred and if provisioning continued at previous levels.
Bar van der Feen of IRIS said although a cut in provisions would boost profits at the banks, EPS would remain about the same due to an increase in shares on issue.
This would be due to the conversion of warrants in ING and convertible preference shares in ABN AMRO.
"The total effect will be about zero," he said.
Heinie Hakker of BZW did not expect a signficant one-off boost to profits, saying the banks would keep provisioning at similar levels to cushion an expected rise in bad loans from current low levels.
He said the most relevant impact of the VAR disclosure was the increase on tier one and tier two capital.
"It gives you a stronger capital base to fund future growth," Hakker said.
Woorm agreed, saying: "You can attract extra capital. That will finance extra growth opportunities."
